technical_and_design_decisions: Reuse Mule's existing transport/component scaffolding (e.g., AbstractTransport, AbstractMessageReceiver) for the new WebSocket components rather than building a brand-new transport layer.
Implement the NIO toggle by extending the existing deploy.properties parser in the bootstrap/launcher module so the property propagates to the transport manager.
Registry integration (U2) is implemented as a new lifecycle phase/agent that registers HTTP endpoints exposed by deployed applications, rather than coupling the Registry client into each transport.
The dynamic lookup component (U3) is implemented as a new router that queries the Registry service for endpoint resolution at runtime, using Mule's existing expression/resolver framework.
Throttling policies (U4) are implemented using Mule's existing policy/filter infrastructure (e.g., a new ThrottlingPolicy) wired into the inbound endpoint lifecycle, with configuration via Registry.
Custom business events and transaction IDs (U5) are surfaced through Mule's existing event/notification API into a new appender that writes to the application log.
MVEL upgrade (U6) is treated as a pure dependency version bump in the parent POM plus regression of DataMapper and any MVEL-using components.
JDBC support for the five new databases (U7) is delivered by extending the existing JDBC connector with type-specific connection URL/driver metadata and validating with live test instances.
SQL query logging (U8) is implemented by adding a configurable DEBUG-level logger around the JDBC connector's PreparedStatement/Statement execution path.
Unit and integration tests are co-located with implementation work (per-activity) plus a final end-to-end integration pass across the increment.
assumptions: Detailed specs linked from U2 and U3 (corp wiki pages) are not accessible; estimates assume the work follows standard Mule patterns (lifecycle agents, routers, registry client).
A single developer performs all work including coding, unit tests, and a final integration test pass.
A workday is 8 hours and estimates include coding + per-activity unit testing + small code-review iterations, but exclude large meeting overhead.
Drivers and connectivity for Oracle, PostgreSQL, Sybase, MS SQL Server, and DB2 are available in the dev environment; no new driver procurement is needed.
WebSocket transport reuses an established Java WebSocket implementation already on the classpath; no new third-party dependency is introduced.
MVEL 2.1.8 is API/source-compatible with the version Mule 3.5.0 currently uses, so the upgrade is a dependency bump plus regression testing.
The existing Registry service exposes the APIs needed for pairing, endpoint registration, dynamic lookup, and throttling policy application.
Throttling policies are delivered as a baseline implementation (e.g., per-endpoint rate limit) and not as a full GUI/CLI policy authoring tool.
Documentation updates are limited to user-facing config and component reference pages; no major architectural docs are produced.

activities.activity_description: Extend the deploy.properties parser so that a new property (e.g., nio.enabled=true) toggles Mule's NIO transport usage at startup, including wiring into the transport factory and a unit test.
Implement WebSocket inbound/outbound message sources and a connector so flows can consume and produce WebSocket messages, including message conversion, lifecycle, and unit tests.
Add configuration support (deploy.properties / Mule config) for the Registry key, including secure handling, and an agent that pairs the ESB instance with the Registry on startup.
On application deployment, discover HTTP endpoints (host/port/path) and register them with the paired Registry, including deregistration on undeployment and error/retries.
